raw_case_text:
A 40-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department following a collapse and was found to have left sided weakness. He denied chest pain, palpitations, dyspnoea or dizziness. He also reported decreased vision is his right eye. Computed tomography (CT) of his head showed a large right fronto-parieto-temporal cortical and subcortical hypodensity involving the right middle cerebral artery territory, producing a mass effect and midline shift of 4.2 mm (Figure 1). CT angiography and head perfusion showed total occlusion of the distal right common carotid artery (Figures 2 and 3). He reported that he had no fever.
On admission his National Institute of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS)   was 18 (a score of 16-20 is considered moderate to severe stroke), so he was not a candidate for thrombolysis. He was assessed by neurosurgery with a decision that no surgical intervention was required as his Glasgow Coma Scale was 15.   The patient declined magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), at that time. The patient underwent serial CT scans and the neurologists were initially very concerned about his haemorrhagic transformation. We waited until they gave clearance.
Blood investigations showed raised haemoglobin of 17.1 g/dL (haemotocrit 51.5) with a slightly reduced protein C activity (59.8%) and normal protein S activity (94.5%) as well as normal antithrombin activity. His protein C resistance was 0.87, and he also had a raised fibrinogen level at 5.25 g/L (normal range 1.7-4.2 g/L). An autoantibody screen was negative. Due to the likelihood of an embolic event, he underwent cardiological assessment. Transthoracic echocardiography showed a highly mobile cystic mass seen in the LVOT (Figures 2 and 3). There was no aortic regurgitation present. Transoesophageal echocardiogram confirmed the cystic mass to be 12 x 8 mm and attached to the undersurface of the non-coronary cusp in the LVOT with normal aortic valve appearance and function (Figures 4 and 5). Hydatid cyst was excluded by serological investigations.
In view of his recent large cerebral infarction, the neurologists decided to wait until his CT scans were favourable, which took 6 weeks. During this time, the patient finally agreed to undergo MRI that confirmed the infarction related to the right middle cerebral artery occlusion with multiple foci of resolving micro-haemorrhages. He underwent CT coronary angiogram, which was normal. Prior to his planned cardiac surgery, cardiac MRI was performed, which suggested no evidence of a LVOT mass. Transthoracic echocardiogram confirmed no residual lesion (Figure 6). Abdominal CT scan showed scarring in the right kidney, secondary to an old insult, although the patient denied ever having abdominal pain. The patient was managed conservatively and continues his rehabilitation, with no recurrence of the mass.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 40-year-old male presented to the Emergency Department following a collapse with left-sided weakness and decreased vision in his right eye.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient collapsed and was brought to the Emergency Department with acute left-sided weakness and decreased vision in his right eye.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for left-sided weakness and decreased right eye vision; negative for chest pain, palpitations, dyspnea, dizziness, fever, or history of abdominal pain.

objective.physical_examination: On admission, Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) was 15 and National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) score was 18 (moderate-to-severe stroke) with left-sided weakness.
objective.routine_investigations: Blood investigations showed elevated hemoglobin of 17.1 g/dL (hematocrit 51.5%), slightly reduced protein C activity (59.8%), normal protein S activity (94.5%), normal antithrombin activity, protein C resistance of 0.87, elevated fibrinogen of 5.25 g/L (normal range 1.7-4.2 g/L), and negative autoantibody screen. Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) revealed a highly mobile cystic mass in the left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) without aortic regurgitation.
objective.advanced_workup: Head CT demonstrated a large right fronto-parieto-temporal cortical and subcortical hypodensity in the right middle cerebral artery (MCA) territory causing mass effect and a 4.2 mm midline shift. CT angiography and head perfusion showed total occlusion of the distal right common carotid artery. Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) confirmed a 12 x 8 mm cystic mass attached to the undersurface of the non-coronary cusp in the LVOT with normal aortic valve appearance and function. Brain MRI performed 6 weeks later confirmed right MCA territory infarction with multiple foci of resolving micro-hemorrhages. CT coronary angiogram was normal. Abdominal CT showed right renal scarring secondary to an old insult. Preoperative cardiac MRI and repeat TTE at 6 weeks showed complete spontaneous resolution of the LVOT mass.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Spontaneous resolution of a left ventricular outflow tract (LVOT) cystic mass (suspected intracardiac thrombosis/cyst) complicated by embolic right common carotid/middle cerebral artery ischemic stroke; cardiac hydatid cyst was excluded by negative serological investigations. The patient was not a candidate for thrombolysis (NIHSS 18) or neurosurgical intervention (GCS 15), and planned cardiac surgery was canceled after cardiac MRI and repeat TTE at 6 weeks confirmed spontaneous disappearance of the LVOT lesion; he was managed conservatively with ongoing stroke rehabilitation and had no recurrence.
